title: Leaders Are Somethin' Else: Behavioural Variation Associated With Roles During Tandem Running Recruitment
content:
In this study, we found moderate to strong repeatabilities in behavioural variables measuring the personality traits: activity, aggressiveness and exploration. Similarly, the probability of acting as a leader during tandem running in an emigration event was moderately (R = 0.469) repeatable. Importantly, individuals with higher levels of activity, exploration and aggressiveness towards conspecifics were more likely to assume the leader role. These results show not only that there are notable interindividual differences in behaviour in Pachycondyla striata ants, but also that certain traits are linked to the leadership role during recruitment, with the potential to increase success while performing this task. These findings contribute to our knowledge about how leadership positions are taken in self-organised social groups, where there is no central control.


ABSTRACT

In social groups, leadership often emerges from consistent interindividual differences in behaviour. Yet how personality shapes role specialisation remains poorly understood. We investigated how personality traits (activity, aggressiveness, boldness and exploration) influence leadership roles in the ant Pachycondyla striata during tandem running, a recruitment strategy where a leader ant guides a single follower to a target destination. Using repeated behavioural assays (open field, novel object, and aggression tests) and forced emigrations, we assessed individual consistency in personality traits and recruitment roles (leader or follower). We found moderate-to-strong repeatability in activity, aggressiveness and exploration, and in the adoption of the leadership role during tandem recruitment. Behavioural responses changed over time: activity decreased after the first trial, suggesting familiarisation with testing contexts or diminishing novelty effects after initial exposures. Tandem runs, and in particular the adoption of the role as a follower, declined sharply in subsequent emigrations as ants transitioned to solitary navigation—a faster strategy once routes were learned. This highlights how experience alters collective decision-making, favouring speed over recruitment. More importantly, more active, exploratory and aggressive ants were significantly more likely to become leaders, suggesting that intrinsic behavioural differences drive task specialisation. By linking personality to role specialisation, this study contributes to a better understanding of how consistent individual variation shapes collective outcomes in social groups. Understanding these mechanisms could provide broader insights into leadership emergence across animal societies.
